opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly a lot of what we did with the energy ratings came directly out of the lessons from model cards and data documentation work.

The biggest thing I learned is that if documentation is too much work, people just won't do it, or they'll do it badly. When model cards first came out, the idea was really ambitious: describe your training data, your intended uses, your limitations, your evaluation across different groups. In practice, a lot of model cards ended up being half-filled templates, or just a couple of lines saying "this is a fine-tuned BERT." It wasn't because people didn't care. It was because nobody gave them the time, the incentives, or the tools to make it easy.

So with the energy work, we tried to lower the barrier as much as possible. Instead of asking developers to measure everything themselves and write it up, we set up a standardized benchmark. You submit your model, it runs on the same hardware, on the same set of tasks, and you get a number back. People don't have to become experts in carbon accounting or GPU power measurement to participate.

The second lesson is that it has to be legible to people who aren't specialists. A model card full of technical details is useful to researchers, but a procurement person or a policymaker needs something they can understand in a few seconds. That's why we went with the star rating idea, a bit like the energy labels on appliances. Everyone knows what five stars versus one star means on a fridge. It's simplified, and you lose some nuance, but you gain a lot in terms of people actually using the information to make decisions.

The third thing is comparability. One frustration with model documentation was that everyone reported things in their own way, so you couldn't really compare across models. With energy, if one company measures inference on an A100 with batch size 64 and another uses completely different hardware and settings, the numbers are meaningless side by side. Standardizing the methodology was really what made it useful.

And finally, incentives matter. Documentation took off more when platforms like Hugging Face made the model card the default landing page for a model. It became visible, so people put effort into it. We're hoping the same thing happens with energy: if the rating is shown where people choose models, developers will want a good score, and that creates a bit of healthy competition toward efficiency.

It's still early, and we're still getting feedback, especially from companies with closed models who are hesitant to participate. But the core lesson is to make it simple, standardized, and visible, otherwise it stays a nice idea that nobody adopts.

r001.rationale: The response says documentation that is too much work or too ambitious leads people to skip it or complete it poorly, and explains that model-card requirements contributed to that burden.

r002.rationale: The response describes submitting a model to run on standardized hardware, implying an externally run assessment, but does not identify users who lack in-house compute as the reason for offering it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the big lesson, honestly, is that if you make it hard, people won't do it. That sounds obvious, but we learned it the hard way with model cards. When model cards first came out, there was a lot of enthusiasm, and the paper was really well cited, but when you actually went and looked at the models being shared on the Hub or on GitHub, most of them either had no card or had one that was basically empty. And it wasn't because people didn't care. It was because writing a model card from a blank page is work, and you're asking a researcher or an engineer who's already shipped the thing to go back and fill out what feels like paperwork.

So what actually moved the needle was lowering the friction. Templates, auto-generated sections, tooling that pulls in whatever metadata it can on its own so the human only has to fill in the parts that genuinely need a human. And making it part of the workflow rather than a separate step. The moment documentation became a thing you do while you're uploading, instead of a thing you do afterward if you remember, adoption went way up.

So with the energy ratings, I tried to bake that in from the start. The whole idea of the Energy Star-style approach is that you don't need to understand the methodology to use it. You see a letter grade or a number of stars, and you get it immediately, the same way you do with a fridge or a washing machine. On the producer side, we built it so that measuring is as close to one line of code as we could get. You wrap your inference, it runs, you get a number, and ideally that number flows straight into the model card. You shouldn't have to install a bunch of hardware monitoring tools and read a paper about PUE to participate.

The other thing I learned is about comparability. Early documentation efforts let everyone describe things in their own words, which is nice for nuance but terrible if you want to compare model A to model B. So with energy we were really deliberate about standardizing the tasks and the hardware setup, because a kilowatt-hour number is meaningless unless you know what it's a kilowatt-hour of. That's why it's organized by task, text generation, image generation, and so on, with a fixed setup, so the comparison actually means something.

And then there's the incentive piece, which documentation efforts have struggled with for years. Nobody gets promoted for writing a great model card. So part of what I'm hoping with the ratings is that making it visible and comparative creates a little bit of healthy competition. If your model gets a worse grade than a comparable one, that's suddenly something people ask about. We've already seen that a bit, developers coming back and saying, okay, how do we get to a better rating. That's the behavior change you want, and you only get it if the thing is simple enough that people actually look at it.

r001.rationale: The response says that hard, blank-page model-card documentation deterred completion and led to missing or empty cards, then describes lowering that friction.

r002.rationale: It describes running an energy measurement by wrapping inference, but does not propose remotely executed assessments for users without in-house compute.

astra-6.text:
One thing we learned from model cards is that you have to make documentation easy to produce and easy to understand. You can create a really thoughtful framework, but if filling it out takes a lot of extra work, adoption is going to be limited.

So with energy ratings, the idea is to automate as much of the measurement as possible and give people a simple result they can use to compare models. You shouldn’t need to be an expert in energy consumption to understand it. But you also need the methodology underneath that label, so someone who wants to dig into what was measured and under what conditions can do that.

And it has to fit into the tools and workflows people already use. If it’s a separate process they have to remember at the end, it’s much easier to skip.

r001.rationale: The response says documentation that takes extra work limits adoption, but it does not identify increasing complexity in data or model documentation as the cause.

r002.rationale: The response mentions automating energy measurements, but does not propose remotely executed assessments for users without in-house compute.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I’ve learned from working on model documentation is that the more you ask people to do, the less likely they are to do it. You can create a really thorough framework, but if filling it out takes a lot of time or requires expertise people don’t have, adoption becomes difficult.

So for energy ratings, the idea is to make the process as automated and straightforward as possible. People shouldn’t have to become experts in energy measurement to understand how their model performs. And on the other side, someone choosing a model should be able to look at a simple rating and get useful information, with the methodology available if they want to dig deeper. There’s a balance between capturing the complexity and giving people something they can actually use.

r001.rationale: It says that asking people to do more, especially completing a time-consuming framework requiring expertise, makes them less likely to participate.

r002.rationale: It advocates making energy ratings automated and straightforward but does not propose remotely executed assessments for users without in-house compute.
